---
title: "Model selection and cross-validation"
description: "GIC presets, information-criterion paths, five-fold CV and the one-SE rule."
output: rmarkdown::html_document
---

The example below has **1,000 observations, 5,000 predictors and 100 nonzero
coefficients of either sign**. It shows a rich coefficient path while retaining
a genuinely sparse underlying model.

```{r design, eval=FALSE}
library(L0glm)
sim <- simul("normal", n=1000L, p=5000L, n_nonzero=100L, seed=42L,
  options=list(beta_range=c(-2, 2)))
X <- sim$X
y <- sim$y
```

## A preset or a tuned path

For a single response the sparse-selection target is

\[
-2\ell(\beta) + \lambda\,\|\beta\|_0.
\]

A preset is often a very effective starting point. Searching a path lets the
data choose among the candidate sparse models.

```{r preset, eval=FALSE}
fit <- l0glmFit(X, y, family=gaussian(), lambda="gic", relaxed=TRUE)
```

| Preset | Penalty per selected coefficient |
|---|---|
| `"aic"` | \(2\) |
| `"bic"` | \(\log n\) |
| `"gic"` | \(\log p\,\log\log n\) |
| `"ebic"` | \(\log n + 2\gamma_{\rm EBIC}\log p\) |
| `"mbic"` | \(\log(np^2/16)\) |

Here `p` counts selectable predictors, excluding intercepts and mandatory terms.
The [information-criterion reference](../reference/information_criteria.html)
gives the parameter-count conventions and literature, including
[Fan & Tang's GIC](https://doi.org/10.1111/rssb.12001).

```{r gic, eval=FALSE}
gic <- l0glmTune(X, y, family=gaussian(), tune="gic", nlambda=10L,
  prop_range=.25, relaxed=TRUE, coefs.true=sim$beta_true, plot=TRUE)
c(lambda_best=gic$lambda_best, lambda_preset=gic$lambda_preset)
```

<img src="../selection-gic.png" alt="One hundred signal coefficients: regularization paths and GIC around the preset." width="100%">

The grid focuses on the preset. Use `prop_range=1` to explore the full numerical
range. The preset often already gives an excellent model, so detailed path
tuning can be reserved for cases where it offers a useful improvement.

<!-- BEGIN selection-metrics -->
| Method | GIC | TP | FP | FN | TN | F1 | MCC |
| --- | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| GIC preset | 5744 | 65 | 0 | 35 | 4900 | 0.788 | 0.803 |
| Tuned GIC | 5536 | 70 | 0 | 30 | 4900 | 0.824 | 0.834 |
| CV minimum | 5539 | 71 | 0 | 29 | 4900 | 0.830 | 0.840 |
| CV one-SE | 5744 | 65 | 0 | 35 | 4900 | 0.788 | 0.803 |

## Five-fold cross-validation

CV selects the penalty with the lowest mean held-out deviance. Whole rows are
held out, including all response channels. Preprocessing, screening and estimated
distribution parameters use the training observations in each fold.
The default `screen="auto"` enables ISIS exactly when `p_eligible > 10*n`,
using the training row count `n` in that fold. The eligible count excludes
mandatory terms and predictors excluded by zero starts in every response
channel. There is no separate minimum sample size or predictor count.

```{r cv, eval=FALSE}
set.seed(10)
folds <- sample(rep(1:5, length.out=nrow(X)))
cv <- l0glmTune(X, y, family=gaussian(), tune="cv", nfolds=5L,
  nlambda=10L, prop_range=.25, foldid=folds, relaxed=TRUE,
  coefs.true=sim$beta_true, plot=TRUE)
```

<img src="../selection-cv.png" alt="Coefficient paths for a sparse 5,000-predictor Gaussian model and five-fold validation deviance with standard-error bars." width="100%">

The curves use a reversed `log10(lambda)` axis: strong regularization is on the
left, and support sizes appear above the panels. CV error bars show one standard error.

```{r selected, eval=FALSE}
c(lambda_best=cv$lambda_best, lambda_1se=cv$lambda_1se,
  lambda_preset=cv$lambda_preset)
predict(cv$fit_1se, X[1:5, , drop=FALSE], type="response")
```

`fit_best` and `fit_1se` are full-data fits. The one-SE rule chooses the largest
lambda with mean deviance within one SE of the minimum. The GIC preset remains
available through `lambda_preset` for comparison.

## Joint tuning of lambda and iteration count

For prediction, early adaptive-ridge estimates can retain useful weak effects.
Pass a vector to `maxit` to select both the penalty and the IRLS iteration limit
by CV. Each pair starts independently, and every candidate uses the same folds.
Screening, normalization and noise estimation use only the training rows.

```{r joint-cv, eval=FALSE}
joint <- l0glmTune(X, y, family=gaussian(), tune="cv", foldid=folds,
  nlambda=10L, prop_range=.25, maxit=c(1:10, 25),
  relaxed=FALSE, local.search=FALSE, plot=TRUE)
c(lambda=joint$lambda_best, maxit=joint$maxit_best)
c(lambda=joint$lambda_1se, maxit=joint$maxit_1se)
joint$metrics[c("lambda", "maxit", "cv_deviance", "cv_se")]
predict(joint$fit_best, X[1:5, , drop=FALSE])
```

The selection minimizes mean held-out deviance over all evaluated
\((\lambda,t)\) pairs. The coefficient panel shows the path at `maxit_best`;
the CV panel shows a curve and standard-error bars for each iteration limit.
The one-SE model uses the largest eligible lambda, then the largest iteration
limit among ties at that lambda. `fit_best` and `fit_1se` use all observations
with their respective selected settings.

A scalar `maxit` keeps ordinary lambda tuning. The limit applies per IRLS
pass, so grouped passes, relaxed refits and local support refinement are
separate stages. Disabling relaxation and local search lets CV compare the
early shrinkage estimates directly. For shorter fits, the upper grid endpoint
can retain nonzero coefficients; the zero endpoint is checked at the largest
iteration limit.

## Optional local support refinement

Set `local.search=TRUE` to test additions, deletions and small predictor
exchanges after fitting. Screening, compulsory-term updates and original-channel
preclustering refits finish first. Every accepted move lowers the fitted
penalty's parameter-count criterion; a supplied independent `validation` set
instead selects by held-out deviance. The original starting exclusions and
coefficient constraints remain in force.

```{r local-support, eval=FALSE}
fit <- l0glmFit(X, y, lambda="gic", local.search="auto")
fit$local.search[c("applied", "initial.size", "stopping")]
fit$local.search$history
gic <- l0glmTune(X, y, family=gaussian(), tune="gic", nlambda=10L,
  local.search="auto", prop_range=.25)
```

`"auto"` limits refinement to models with at most 50 coefficient dimensions
after the initial fit. For grouped multichannel fits, each selected row counts
its channel dimensions; multinomial rows have one fewer dimension because of
their zero-sum constraint. The limit is set with `control.local$size.max`.
`"auto"` is the default; `FALSE` disables refinement. See the [controls](../reference/local_search.html)
and [benchmark examples](performance.html#abess-benchmark-problems).

IC paths rank ordinary and special-family models using the same counts as
`GIC()`, `AIC()` and the other criterion methods. CV independently refines each
training fit before evaluating its held-out fold; validation fold responses
do not enter the support search.

## Random, contiguous and Venetian-blind folds

Without `foldid`, folds are randomly assigned. Supply a vector to choose a design:

```{r folds, eval=FALSE}
# Five contiguous blocks
folds <- rep(1:5, length.out=nrow(X))[order(rep(1:5, length.out=nrow(X)))]

# Venetian blind: odd and even observations alternate
folds <- rep(1:2, length.out=nrow(X))
cv <- l0glmTune(X, y, family=gaussian(), tune="cv",
  foldid=folds, nlambda=10, relaxed=TRUE)
```

For time-dependent observations, choose folds that reflect how predictions
will be used. Reserve an independent test set when measuring final predictive accuracy.

## Compare methods

`sparseGLM()` supplies one comparison interface for L0glm, ABESS, L0Learn,
LASSO, relaxed LASSO, adaptive variants, MCP and SCAD where supported. The
optional biglasso adapter also fits plain LASSO directly on double bigmemory
designs; see the [file-backed example](file-backed.html#compare-with-native-file-backed-lasso).

```{r compare, eval=FALSE}
comparison <- sparseGLM(X, y, family=gaussian(),
  method=c("L0glm", "abess", "lasso", "relaxed_lasso"),
  tune="cv", nfolds=5, foldid=sample(rep(1:5, length.out=nrow(X))), nlambda=10)
l0glmMetrics(comparison)
```

`method="all"` expands to supported methods for the requested model.
The [benchmark article](performance.html) reports complete fitting and tuning times.
